quadHead: Four ways Malaysia catches tourists off guard.

quad.title: The KLIA 'Teksi Sapu' Switch
quad.tl: An unbadged man in arrivals quotes RM350 to your KLCC hotel; the real Grab fare is RM65–RM95 and the official budget-taxi coupon is RM84.30. In October 2025 one illegal KLIA2 driver was fined RM5,000 for charging a tourist RM836.

quad.title: The Pantai Cenang Jet-Ski Trap
quad.tl: A beach stall rents a jet-ski for RM150 with no pre-ride photo, then 'finds' a chipped nose cone and demands RM500–RM2,000 cash — four or five 'friends' appear if you refuse.

quad.title: The Jonker Walk QR-Code Switch
quad.tl: A fake DuitNow QR sticker is pasted over the real one at a satay stall, so your RM35 tap lands in a mule account. One Melaka couple ran the script across petrol stations and grocers for close to RM3,000.

quad.title: The Jesselton Point Island-Hop
quad.tl: A tout near Suria Sabah pitches 'five islands, snorkel and lunch, RM200' on an unlicensed boat — snorkel, lunch and park entry are all extra, and a stranded return can cost another RM100–RM200 cash. The real 3-island trip is RM80–RM120.

body: Malaysia: Tourist Scams is part of the tabiji.ai Travel Safety Series. Every scam is documented against Malaysian sources — the Royal Malaysia Police (PDRM 999), the National Scam Response Centre (997), Tourism Malaysia notices and the JPJ teksi-sapu line — plus r/Malaysia reports and verified reporting from the New Straits Times, The Star and Malay Mail. Sourced, not recycled.

60 specific scams across Kuala Lumpur, Penang, Melaka, Langkawi, Kota Kinabalu and five more destinations. The exact scripts, the red flags that give them away, and the Bahasa Malaysia phrases that shut them down — written so you can show them on your phone.
Scams evolve, so the book is re-researched every year, and the current edition sits in your Kindle library. Built for the traveler who wants to move through Malaysia relaxed, not braced.
